Case study · Interactive software development

Repository Public

Focus Interactive systems

title: Tower Defense Game
text:
Project overview
The repository names the application TowerDefend. It is a public React and TypeScript project with a dedicated game-engine layer and a component-based interface. Its source includes game entities, state and rendering modules, achievement and upgrade systems, an Express production entry point, and progressive-web-app configuration.

title: Tower Defense Game
text:
Problem / goal
The project’s goal is to create an interactive browser game whose real-time mechanics, progression systems, interface state, and persistent player data remain coordinated as the application grows.

title: Tower Defense Game
text:
What I built
The game engine manages waves, enemies, towers, bullets, collisions, targeting, rewards, and upgrade effects. Supporting modules handle achievements, player statistics, skill progression, audio, and browser storage, while React components provide the surrounding dashboard and controls.
The Vite PWA configuration adds an install prompt and offline app-shell caching. The repository documents local development, production builds, and static deployment preparation; it does not claim a live demo yet.

text:

→

02 Game engine Wave timing, targeting, collisions, and rewards

→

03 Progression systems Statistics, skills, upgrades, and achievements

→

04 Browser persistence Local player state and PWA app shell

text:

TypeScript game loop with separate engine, entity, state, HUD, and renderer modules
Wave-based enemy spawning and tower targeting
Upgrade, skill, achievement, and player-stat systems

title: Tower Defense Game
text:
What I learned
The project demonstrates how real-time state differs from conventional page state. Game mechanics, rendering, progression, and interface feedback need clear boundaries while still responding to the same event loop and persistent player model.

title: Tower Defense Game
text:
Future improvements
The repository does not include automated tests and marks the live demo as forthcoming. Useful next steps would be testing progression rules, profiling performance across devices, and publishing the prepared production build.

title: CedHealth
text:
Project overview
CedHealth is a public health-tracking application built with Python and Flask. Its repository contains a server application, SQLite data access, Jinja templates, a web manifest, a service worker, and a Gunicorn production entry point.
The application organizes several related health workflows behind user accounts instead of treating meals, goals, and workouts as disconnected tools.

title: CedHealth
text:
Problem / goal
The project’s goal is to provide one place for users to establish personal goals and record health-related activity. The interface needs to support multiple workflows while maintaining user-specific data between sessions.

title: CedHealth
text:
What I built
The source implements authentication and onboarding, a dashboard, goal management, meal and weight logging, workout and exercise views, favorites, saved meals, and nutrition-oriented lookup and analysis routes.
It also includes a web app manifest and service worker so the Flask application can provide an installable progressive-web-app experience.

title: About
text:
About me



I’m Cedric Martin, a Business Analytics student at BYU–Idaho interested in the intersection of analytics, finance, software, and business systems.

title: About
text:
How I approach analytics
I’m drawn to work that begins with a practical business question and ends with something people can actually use: a clean dataset, a repeatable workflow, a clear report, or a better way to make a decision.
My approach combines business context with hands-on technical work. I enjoy understanding how information moves through an organization, finding where inconsistent data or manual effort gets in the way, and building structured solutions with tools such as Python, SQL, and Power BI.
Finance and FP&A are especially interesting to me because they connect detailed analysis to planning and performance. More broadly, I’m motivated by roles where analytical thinking can improve how a business operates.


01

Start with the decision
Good analysis is shaped by the question it needs to answer.



02

Build for reliability
Clear structure, validation, and documentation make analytical work more useful.



03

Communicate clearly
The value of analysis depends on whether others can understand and act on it.

title: Aster Desktop Assistant
text:
Project overview
Aster is a Windows desktop assistant built in Python. The private source is organized into separate modules for the user interface, AI responses, action routing, permissions, external information services, local learning state, watchlists, news briefings, and shared sessions.
This case study remains intentionally high-level: it describes the application architecture without exposing credentials, configuration values, or private source code.

title: Aster Desktop Assistant
text:
Problem / goal
The project explores how a desktop assistant can support more than open-ended conversation. Its structure connects natural-language requests to useful desktop and information tasks while keeping system actions explicit and permission-aware.

title: Aster Desktop Assistant
text:
What I built
The application includes a PySide6 interface, an OpenAI-backed response layer, a structured action router, a permission manager, environment-based integration configuration, and local stores for saved state, learning concepts, and watchlist items.
The source also includes economic and company dashboard workflows, categorized news briefings, voice-related dependencies, Excel workbook actions, and host/client shared chat sessions.

→

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Case study · Business analytics



A local Windows application for turning marketplace and internal sales exports into a standardized, traceable event ledger for review and downstream analysis.


Focus Data preparation & quality


Tools Python, Flask, SQL Server, Power BI


Context Real business sales data



Private repository — project summary available publicly.

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Project summary
Core 4x4 is a real-business analytics project centered on marketplace and internal sales data arriving in different export formats. The repository implements a local Windows application that turns those inputs into a standardized, traceable event ledger.
The workflow supports file-type detection, product and SKU mapping, exact-file and business-record duplicate handling, validation reports, optional SQL Server loading, and analytics views for Power BI. Proprietary records and business details are intentionally excluded from this public case study.

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Business problem
Sales information from separate platforms can differ in structure, naming conventions, product identifiers, and record quality. Without a consistent preparation process, those differences make it harder to combine records and use them reliably in reporting.
The project addresses the need for a shared analytical foundation: one that preserves the useful information in each source while applying common business rules before analysis.

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
My approach
I approached the project as a data reliability problem rather than a simple file-conversion task. I reviewed source structures, built Python transformation and identity logic, defined validation behavior, implemented approved product and SKU mapping, and prepared SQL and Power BI assets around the resulting event ledger.
Specific organizational details, credentials, and proprietary records are intentionally omitted.

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Architecture
The application separates source adapters, a canonical event schema, shared validation and mapping rules, batch orchestration, and controlled delivery steps. Users can process files through a local desktop or browser interface, review warnings, save a standardized CSV and validation report, and optionally load an approved result into SQL Server for Power BI.

Design principle
Separate source-specific cleanup from shared business rules. This makes the workflow easier to reason about and extend when a source changes or a new one is introduced.

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Data workflow


01 Source files Tested eBay and Core 4x4 exports, plus approved SKU mappings

→

02 Ingest & standardize Align fields, formats, and data types

→

03 Map products Apply approved SKU mappings without changing source identifiers

→

04 Deduplicate Separate exact file copies from repeated business records

→

05 Validate & deliver Save reports or load approved data for Power BI

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Key technical decisions


Preserve event meaning
The canonical schema keeps record_type separate from row grain so order lines and standalone financial events—such as fees, payouts, holds, and refunds—are not forced into the same meaning.


Separate identity levels
The pipeline uses a file hash for exact uploaded bytes and a business record_key for cross-file deduplication. Those identifiers answer different questions and remain separate.


Keep legitimate repeats
Rows with the same logical identity receive occurrence-aware record keys in source order. Repeated real events remain distinct, while a harmlessly resaved report reproduces the same sequence of keys.


Control mapping
Only explicitly approved SKU mappings populate the standardized SKU. Suggested, missing, or conflicting mappings remain visible for review instead of being silently accepted.

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Data quality and validation
Source detection uses report-column signatures rather than filenames. Unsupported or uncertain files require manual source selection, and questionable rows are preserved with either warning or review_needed status instead of being silently discarded.
The output retains provenance fields for the import run, source file, system, report, row number, and adapter version. Automated tests cover schema consistency, long text identifiers, duplicate files, cross-file business duplicates, occurrence-aware record identity, approved mapping behavior, SQL contracts, and Power BI assets. Database integration tests are available separately when SQL Server is configured.

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Key capabilities

Source adapters for tested eBay and Core 4x4 exports
Automatic source detection with a manual selection fallback
Canonical event ledger with source lineage and occurrence-aware record keys
Approved SKU mapping from XLSX or CSV files
Exact-file and business-record duplicate handling
Validation reports with warning and review-needed records
Transactional SQL Server loading for approved runs
Purpose-specific SQL analytics views and documented Power BI measures
Provisional Amazon adapter that remains unvalidated without a representative sample

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Tools and technologies

PythonFlaskOpenPyXLSQL ServerSQLPower BIDAXData Validation

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Business value
The pipeline provides a consistent foundation for sales analysis by making source differences, lineage, mapping rules, duplicate handling, and validation explicit parts of a repeatable process. Analysts can review file and record outcomes before an approved run is stored for downstream reporting.
No quantitative performance or financial claims are included because those outcomes have not been established for publication.

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
What I learned
This project reinforced that dependable analytics begins before a dashboard is built. Source context, naming conventions, product identity, and validation rules all shape whether an analytical output can be trusted.
It also highlighted the importance of designing workflows in stages. A modular process makes it easier to isolate issues, revise business rules, and communicate how raw information becomes a reporting dataset.

title: Core 4x4 Analytics Data Pipeline
text:
Future improvements
The repository identifies real-sample Amazon validation, cross-source order reconciliation, and continued operational hardening as future work. Amazon support remains provisional until representative exports pass the same detection, transformation, and validation checks as the tested sources.
